newsitem.title: USA: Central bank gold sale talk not whole picture - WGC.
newsitem.headline: Central bank gold sale talk not whole picture - WGC.

text.p: The perennial buzz about rumored central bank gold sales have rattled prices, but the market has tended to forget about official purchases of gold, producer lobby World Gold Council said.
"The rumors and fears of central banks sales were very damaging to the gold price," World Gold Council economic advisor Richard Scott-Ram said.
But the stronger dollar had also helped to weaken gold tags, he said. "We have also seen huge short positions and that's been very damaging to gold prices."
"But we must be very careful not to generalise that all central banks in the world dislike gold," he added.

"We never hear about purchases of gold by central banks in the Far East and the many other countries such as Russia and the republics in Russia that continue to hold gold," Scott-Ram said at a briefing for reporters.
Russia's central bank has said it will add some 100 tonnes to reserves this year and next.

In addition, the Swiss had yet to hold their referendum on transferring some reserves to a humanitarian fund, and the International Monetary Fund may not sell a single ounce as any proposal to do so is constantly delayed, Scott-Ram said.
The Council said in a report Wednesday that first quarter gold demand rose 17 percent to 770.6 tonnes.

The official sector remained the single most important influence on the gold market in the first quarter, with feared sales by central banks undermining investor confidence and encouraging speculative short selling.
"In spite of all the speculation, there were no reports of any substantial sales of gold by central banks during the first quarter of 1997," the report added.
Scott-Ram said gold was also still an attractive investment vehicle despite low inflation.
Gold has traditionally attracted money, the so-called flight to quality, when inflation threatens to rear its head.
"Our basic message to institutions is that you should buy gold as a portfolio asset. It's very liquid and it's competitive," Scott-Ram said.
The Council's report said demand was spurred in part by lower gold prices. But tags would have to rise sharply to dampen demand in jewelry, Council officials said.
"In the developed markets it would take a $50 (an ounce) increase in the price of gold before retailers would raise prices," officials said.
In the developing markets, people tended to buy into rising prices, they added.
The rise and fall of a country's gross national product was still the key determinant of gold demand, the Council said.
"Our gold market is not falling apart - we have very strong underlying demand and that will help us keep the price up," Scott-Ram said.
